newsitem.title: USA: Lockheed Martin not pursuing Airbus - source.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed Martin not pursuing Airbus - source.

text.p: Lockheed Martin Corp is not holding merger talks with European consortium Airbus Industrie and does not plan to partner with the group in its development of a superjumbo jet, according to a source familiar with the U.S. company.

The source, who did not want to be identified, dismissed a Saturday report in Britain's Times newspaper that said the two groups were holding merger talks in an attempt to battle market dominance by Boeing Co.

Although Lockheed Martin is involved in many ventures with companies around the world, "these initiatives do not include merger or acquisition discussions with Airbus Industrie," the source said, adding the company has "no intention of becoming a major equity investor in the commercial aircraft business."
Maryland-based Lockheed Martin declined to comment specifically on the Airbus rumor, stressing only that it is pursuing a wide variety of alliances.

"Lockheed Martin is a global company and, as such, we are exploring a series of initiatives and opportunities with companies around the world. These include partnerships, strategic alliances and program-specific arrangements that are mutually beneficial across our diverse businesses," according to a statement issued by the company.

The report in the British newspaper prompted little reaction among U.S. analysts, who immediately dismissed the notion. They noted that Airbus is a marketing consortium and will not be turned into an integrated company until 1999.

The Airbus partners are Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace and Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA). Lockheed Martin already is involved in projects with the individual partners and that is likely to continue, the source said.
The source also said Lockheed Martin had no plans to produce commercial aircraft although it would continue supplying various parts.
Airbus, which is in the early stages of developing the A3XX superjumbo aircraft, is widely expected to link up with other companies on the project.

"It goes without question they need some help. Airbus alone does not have the resources, either financially or in manufacturing, to do this on its own. The magnitude of this endeavor requires global partners and suppliers," said Peter Jacobs of Ragen MacKenzie.
